hints: Think about how many particles have zero energy and how many have very high energy, then sketch what that means for where the curve starts and ends.
Recall what is counted on each axis when you plot how particle energies are spread out at one temperature.
walkthrough:
Picture what the distribution means**
Imagine you could freeze the krypton sample and count how many atoms have each energy. Almost no atoms are standing completely still, so almost none have zero energy. Most have a middling energy near the peak, and only a few have very large energy. That is why your curve must start at the origin.

Get the characteristic shape right**
Let the curve climb quickly from (0,0) to a peak, then fall away more slowly to the right with a long tail. It must get closer and closer to the horizontal axis at high energy but never actually touch it, because there is always a tiny chance of a very energetic particle. It also never touches the vertical axis except at the origin.

Final answer: Curve labelled T1 starts at origin, rises steeply to a maximum then falls gradually towards the energy axis, approaching but never touching the axis.
Vertical axis: number of particles (or fraction / probability); horizontal axis: (kinetic / particle) energy.

hints: Think about what heating does to average energy and to the spread of energies, and how the total area under the curve must stay the same.
walkthrough:
Shift and flatten for higher temperature**
When you heat the gas the average energy moves up, so the peak slides to the right. The energies also spread out more, so the peak must drop down to keep the total number of particles, which is the total area under the curve, constant. Draw T2 starting at the same origin, peaking lower and to the right of T1, then staying above T1 out in the high energy tail.
Final answer: Second curve labelled T2 starts at origin, with a lower maximum shifted to the right (higher energy) compared to T1, and a broader tail. Total area under curve same as T1.

hints: Think about the two ways real particles differ from ideal points, their own size and the attractions between them.
Think about what happens when ideal particles hit each other or the wall, and whether any kinetic energy is lost.
walkthrough:
Remove size and attraction**
An ideal gas is a simplified model. First, pretend each krypton atom is a point with no volume of its own, so the container volume is all free space. Second, pretend there are no attractions or repulsions between atoms at all, so they move independently except when they collide.

Make collisions perfect**
Add the collision rule. When ideal particles collide with each other or the wall, no kinetic energy is lost overall, the collisions are perfectly elastic. Pick any two of these ideas to state clearly for your two marks.

Final answer: Any two from:
No intermolecular / van der Waals forces between particles.
Volume of particles is negligible compared to volume of container.
Collisions with other particles and container walls are perfectly elastic.
Particles behave as rigid spheres with random motion.

hints: Start by converting the 2.00 g of krypton into moles using $A_r$ of krypton, about 83.8.
List $p$, $V$, $n$, $R$ and $T$ for $pV=nRT$ and convert temperature to kelvin and volume to $\text{m}^3$ so pressure comes out in Pa.
Rearrange to $p = nRT/V$ and check your power of ten from $\text{dm}^3$ to $\text{m}^3$ before calculating.
walkthrough:
Find moles of krypton**
Moles links mass to the gas equation. Use $$n = \frac{m}{M_r}$$ with $m = 2.00 \text{ g}$ and $M_r = 83.8$: $$n = \frac{2.00}{83.8} = 0.02387 \text{ mol}$$ Keep extra figures for now.

Put everything in SI units for Pa**
For pressure in Pa you need $V$ in $\text{m}^3$ and $T$ in K. Convert: $$T = 120 + 273 = 393 \text{ K}$$ $$V = 5.00 \text{ dm}^3 = 5.00 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$$ $R = 8.31 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$ is already correct.

Apply $pV = nRT$**
Rearrange to $$p = \frac{nRT}{V}$$ Substitute: $$p = \frac{0.02387 \times 8.31 \times 393}{5.00 \times 10^{-3}}$$ $$p = 1.56 \times 10^4 \text{ Pa}$$ That is about $15600 \text{ Pa}$ to three significant figures, matching your data.

hints: Recall whether high or low pressure pushes particles close together, and whether high or low temperature gives them high kinetic energy.
Link each condition back to one ideal assumption, negligible volume or no attractions.
walkthrough:
State the pair of conditions**
Krypton is most ideal at low pressure and high temperature. Learn that as a pair, they work together to make the real gas look like the ideal model.

Explain why each helps**
At low pressure the atoms are far apart in a large space, so their own tiny volume is negligible next to the container volume. At high temperature they move very fast with large kinetic energy, so any weak van der Waals attractions between them are too small to matter and collisions are effectively elastic.

Final answer: Low pressure and high temperature.
At low pressure the volume of particles is negligible compared to container volume. At high temperature particles have high kinetic energy so van der Waals forces are insignificant.

hints: Use the sign of $\Delta H_f = +60.2 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ to decide whether the product level for $\text{KrF}_2$ sits above or below the reactant level.
Remember $E_a$ is measured from reactants up to the top of the hump, not from products, and $\Delta H$ is the vertical gap between reactants and products.
walkthrough:
Place reactants and products for an endothermic step**
$\Delta H_f = +60.2 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ is positive, so energy is absorbed. Draw a horizontal line for products clearly above the given reactants line. Then join them with a smooth hump that peaks well above both, because the reaction goes in one step.

Label the two energy gaps**
Mark $E_a$ as the vertical arrow from the reactants level up to the very top of the hump. That gap is $+385 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Mark $\Delta H_f$ as the vertical arrow from the reactants level up to the products level. That smaller gap is $+60.2 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Final answer: Products ($\text{KrF}_2$) level drawn higher than reactants level by $\Delta H_f$. Curve rises from reactants to a peak then falls to products.
$E_a$ labelled as reactants to peak (+385 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$), $\Delta H_f$ labelled as reactants to products (+60.2 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$).

hints: Start with the observed effect on rate when temperature is raised.
Connect higher temperature to the Boltzmann distribution and the fraction of collisions that can clear the $E_a$ barrier.
walkthrough:
Give the rate change**
Heating always speeds this reaction up, so state clearly that rate increases. The key is not just that particles move faster and collide more often, but that many more collisions are useful.

Use $E_a$ as the hurdle**
For reaction, colliding $\text{Kr}$ and $\text{F}_2$ must meet with at least the activation energy and with correct orientation. At higher temperature the Boltzmann distribution flattens and shifts right, so a much larger fraction now has $E \geqslant E_a$. That gives a much higher frequency of successful collisions per unit time, so rate rises sharply.

Final answer: Rate increases.
Higher temperature means a greater proportion of particles have energy greater than or equal to $E_a$, so frequency of successful collisions increases.
